*   Input data array $A$ in a-order (row-major) layout [S3, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly defines 'a-order' as a row-major layout where adjacent indices in the first dimension (e.g., A[i, j] and A[i+1, j]) are adjacent in physical memory, while indices in the second dimension (e.g., A[i, j] and A[i, j+1]) are far apart. This matches the definition provided in the claim.

*   Memory inflation for non-power-of-two dimensions [S3, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states in the 'A word of warning' section and Section 2.3 that the z-order layout method works best with dimensions that are even powers of two. It further warns that when input data is not an even power of two in size, there will be an 'inflation of the memory footprint' because padding is applied to align with the power-of-two requirements of the Z-order curve. This directly supports the claim that memory inflation occurs for non-power-of-two dimensions.

Z-order curve flattening is a locality-preserving memory layout technique that maps 3D voxel coordinates to a 1D linear index using a space-filling curve, placing spatially adjacent voxels in contiguous memory [S1][S2, unofficial].

The claim states that Z-order curve flattening is a locality-preserving memory layout technique that maps 3D voxel coordinates to a 1D linear index using a space-filling curve, placing spatially adjacent voxels in contiguous memory. Source [S1] explicitly identifies the Morton/z-order curve as a 'space filling curve' used for 'locality-preserving data access patterns' to optimize disk access by arranging data in a 'continuous layout'. Source [S2] explicitly describes the Z-order curve as a 'flattening function' that 'converts 3D voxel coordinates to a 1D index' (implied by the context of flattening functions and linear indexing) and states that it 'place[s] voxels that are nearby in space nearby in memory'. Both sources confirm the core components of the claim: the use of the Z-order curve as a flattening/mapping technique, its locality-preserving nature, and the mapping of spatial proximity to memory proximity.

The method follows three phases: Initialization, Conversion, and Access [S3, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly outlines a three-phase usage pattern for the zorder-lib library. Section 2.1 states: 'Typical use will consist of first performing some one-time initialization (Sec. 2.2), data conversion from a-order to z-order format (Sec. 2.3), then accessing array elements from memory to perform the desired computations (Sec 2.4).' The subsequent sections detail these phases: 2.2 Initialization (calling zoInitZOrderIndexing), 2.3 Data Conversion (calling zoConvertArrayOrderToZOrder), and 2.4 Accessing Data (using routines like zoGetIndex to access elements). Thus, the claim that the method follows these three phases is fully supported by the text.

It further illustrates this with code showing `off_t indx;` being used to access the array directly (`d = data[indx];`). This confirms that the linear index is a 64-bit integer offset (assuming standard `off_t` size on the platform, which is implied by the context of 64-bit systems like Intel Knight's Corner mentioned) representing the position in the 1D array.

*   Grid dimensions $(M_x, M_y, M_z)$, ideally even powers of two [S3, unofficial].

The claim states that grid dimensions $(M_x, M_y, M_z)$ are ideally even powers of two, citing source [S3]. The provided text from Source [S3] explicitly states: 'A word of warning: the z-order layout method has an intrinsic limitation, which is that it really wants to work only with data that is an even power of two in size in each dimension.' It further explains that while the implementation functions with non-power-of-two sizes, it causes significant memory footprint inflation. Therefore, the evidence supports the claim that even powers of two are the ideal dimensions.
